The Battle of Marengo. On June 14, 1800, in the Piedmont region of northern Italy, one of Napoleon's most celebrated early victories took place. Approximately 28,000 French troops faced 35,000 Austrian forces near the village of Marengo. The Austrian general Michael von Melas attacked aggressively in the morning and initially drove the French back. By midday, Napoleon was nearly routed and contemplated retreat. A powerful flanking counterattack by French general Desaix, killed during the assault, shattered the Austrian formation and turned the battle decisively. Austrian losses were approximately 14,000 casualties and prisoners. French losses were around 6,000 but inflicted strategically decisive damage on the enemy. The Treaty of Lunéville followed, confirming French control of Italy and the left bank of the Rhine, establishing French hegemony in western Europe. Marengo boosted Napoleon's political authority at home and solidified his position as First Consul. It became his personal favorite among his victories and restored French control of Italy after a period of Austrian gains. The battle demonstrated the value of tactical flexibility and the ability to recover from tactical adversity through bold maneuver. It was a pivotal early victory that secured Napoleon's power and became a cornerstone of Napoleonic legend.
